raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old male migrant from the Gambia presented in 2019 with epigastric pain, a history of weight loss and fatigue to the University Hospital of Bern, Switzerland. He denied fever, cough, and night sweats. There was no nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea reported. In the medical history, he reported that he was treated for pulmonary TB twice in the Gambia, approximately 5 and 10 years ago for 6 and 8 months, respectively.
The vital parameters and the clinical exam were unremarkable. Full blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, and liver function tests were normal. HIV serology was negative, as was a Helicobacter pylori antigen test of the stool. Further workup followed with a CXR and an abdominal ultrasound. While the ultrasound showed no abnormality, the CXR revealed consolidation in the upper zone of the right lung and was described as suspicious for pulmonary TB by the local radiologist (Fig. 1).
A CT chest demonstrated a dense nodular consolidation in the apex of the right lung and a small cavitary lesion with discrete tree-in-bud and ground glass opacification surrounding the cavity (Fig. 2). The CT scan findings supported the suspected recurrent episode of TB.
Further workup for active pulmonary TB was initiated. Smear microscopy and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) diagnostics (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, US) from sputum samples were negative. Subsequently, a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed, which detected Mtb. DNA with a "trace" on quantification. Resistance to rifampicin was reported as "indeterminate" due to low quantity of Mtb. DNA. The result of the BAL prompted us to repeat an analysis from sputum on the next day, which was now reported as Mtb. DNA "very low", and rifampicin resistance was detected. Due to the clinical implications of this result, a second BAL was performed. PCR results revealed Mtb. DNA "trace", rifampicin resistance "indeterminate" and endobronchial brushing yielded Mtb. DNA "low", and no rifampicin resistance was detected (Table 1).
This complex diagnostic scenario allowed the following conclusion: in a patient with two previous episodes of TB disease and new onset of TB symptoms (weight loss and fatigue) a minimal amount of Mtb. DNA was detectable, potentially with the presence of mutations, conferring resistance to rifampicin. The options to initiate treatment for drug-resistant TB or to await Mtb. cultures were discussed. Nevertheless, considering the social circumstances of the patient and the challenges of adherence and management of side effect of drug-resistant TB treatment and the negligible risk of contagiousness with only "trace" or "very low" quantity Mtb. DNA on PCR test, we opted for a further diagnostic workup to understand the metabolic activity of the detected lung lesions.
Based on the inflammatory characteristics of active TB disease, a [18F]2-fluoro-2-deoxy-d-glucose (FDG) positron emission tomography CT scan (PET/CT) was performed to evaluate the metabolic activity of the pulmonary lesions. The PET/CT demonstrated high FDG uptake (SUVmax 9.06 SUVbw, total lung glycolysis (TLG) of 151.62 SUVbw*ml) with a total lesion volume above SUV = 1 of 63.0 ml of the apical lesion of the right lung, suggesting a highly inflamed and active process as opposed to cold lesions that have been described as scarred tissue of previous TB (Fig. 2). The decision was taken to perform a CT-guided biopsy of the lesion with the highest FDG uptake: despite demonstrating granulomatous tissue Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and smear microscopy of the tissue sample remained negative.
Those results led to the decision, to not start treatment for drug resistant TB (MDR-TB), but to await TB culture results (Bactec MGIT, Becton Dickenson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, US). The patient was subsequently discharged from our hospital, his abdominal symptoms had subsided, and no other reason for the weight loss and fatigue could be established. TB cultures from all collected sputum, BAL brushing, and biopsy specimen remained negative after prolonged incubation (12 weeks, Table 1). Unfortunately, the patient could not be traced for follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male migrant from the Gambia presented with epigastric pain, weight loss, and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in 2019 to the University Hospital of Bern with epigastric pain, unintentional weight loss, and fatigue.
subjective.past_medical_history: Migrant from the Gambia; treated twice previously for pulmonary tuberculosis in the Gambia approximately 10 and 5 years prior for 8 and 6 months, respectively.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for epigastric pain, weight loss, and fatigue; negative for fever, cough, night sweats, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Vital parameters and physical examination were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, and liver function tests were normal. HIV serology and stool Helicobacter pylori antigen test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Chest X-ray revealed consolidation in the right upper lung zone suspicious for pulmonary TB.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated a dense nodular consolidation in the right lung apex and a small cavitary lesion with surrounding tree-in-bud and ground-glass opacification. Initial sputum smear microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra PCR were negative. First BAL Xpert Ultra detected 'trace' M. tuberculosis DNA (rifampicin resistance indeterminate); repeat sputum Xpert Ultra detected 'very low' M. tuberculosis DNA with rifampicin resistance; second BAL detected 'trace' DNA (rifampicin indeterminate) and endobronchial brushing detected 'low' DNA without rifampicin resistance. 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense metabolic activity in the right apical lesion (SUVmax 9.06, TLG 151.62 SUVbw*mL, metabolic volume 63.0 mL). CT-guided biopsy of the FDG-avid right apical lesion showed granulomatous tissue, but tissue smear microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: In a patient with two prior episodes of treated pulmonary TB, persistent trace/very-low residual M. tuberculosis DNA on respiratory Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra with discordant rifampicin resistance calls and FDG-avid apical granulomatous inflammation on PET/CT was evaluated without immediate initiation of MDR-TB therapy while awaiting liquid mycobacterial cultures (BACTEC MGIT). All sputum, BAL, endobronchial brushing, and lung biopsy cultures remained negative after 12 weeks of incubation, ruling out active culture-positive TB relapse; the patient's epigastric pain resolved prior to discharge, though he was subsequently lost to follow-up.
